content: Dr. George A. Sheehan, born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1918, was a renowned figure in the world of running and sports literature. He gained widespread recognition for his books and writings on the subject of running, with his most famous work, Running & Being: The Total Experience, achieving New York Times bestseller status. During his college years, he excelled as a track athlete and later pursued a career in medicine, becoming a cardiologist like his father. During World War II, Dr. Sheehan served as a physician in the United States Navy aboard the destroyer USS Daly (DD-519) in the South Pacific. He married Mary Jane Fleming, and together they raised twelve children. Despite being diagnosed with prostate cancer later in life, he continued to write prolifically, even as he battled the disease. His final book, Going the Distance, was published shortly after his death in 1993. Dr. Sheehan was the eldest of 14 children. Although he was a track star at Manhattan College, he did not rekindle his passion for running until the age of 45, while living in Rumson, New Jersey. He began running in his backyard, completing 26 loops to cover a mile, and later took to running along the river road during his lunch breaks, often wearing long underwear and a ski mask. Remarkably, at the age of 50, he ran a mile in 4 minutes and 47 seconds, becoming the first person in the world over 50 to break the five-minute mile barrier. He started writing a weekly column for a local newspaper, a commitment he maintained for 25 years. Many of these years were spent as the medical editor for Runner's World magazine, a role he took on after being introduced to Joe Henderson by Hal Higdon during the 1968 Olympics. Henderson later recruited him for the position. Dr. Sheehan continued to contribute to Runner's World even after the magazine was acquired by Rodale Press. Over the course of his life, he authored eight books and delivered lectures around the globe. A devout Catholic, Dr. Sheehan co-founded Christian Brothers Academy, an all-male preparatory school in Lincroft, New Jersey, in 1958. The school, located near his home in Rumson, grew to become one of New Jersey's premier prep schools. In 1986, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer but continued running until his physical condition no longer allowed it. During this time, he shifted his focus to writing about his experiences with illness and mortality, rather than running. His final book, Going the Distance, explored these themes and was published shortly after his passing in 1993.
